nameStory: The canvasback gets its name from its distinctive back coloring, which resembles the pale gray canvas cloth once used for sails and tents. Early hunters and naturalists thought the bird's finely barred back looked just like woven canvas fabric stretched across its body.
description: The canvasback is North America's largest diving duck, with a sleek, athletic build perfect for underwater hunting. Males sport a rich chestnut-red head and neck, black chest, and that famous canvas-gray back, while females are brownish overall with a warm rusty head. These powerful ducks have a distinctive wedge-shaped profile created by their sloping forehead that flows smoothly into a long, dark bill. They're substantial birds, noticeably larger and longer than most other diving ducks you'll see.

idTips.label: Sloping profile
idTips.description: The head flows in an unbroken line from the crown down to the tip of the long, dark bill - no forehead bump like other diving ducks. This creates a distinctive wedge or ski-slope silhouette that's visible even at great distances.

idTips.label: Male's canvas back
idTips.description: The pale gray back has fine black lines that create a woven canvas texture you can see with binoculars. The back contrasts sharply with the black chest and rich reddish-brown head.

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably bigger and more robust than ring-necked ducks or scaup - about the size of a small goose. They sit high on the water and appear long and lean.

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Warm brown overall with a rusty-cinnamon head and neck. The back is grayish-brown and the distinctive sloping head profile is still obvious.

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Long, dark bill that appears almost spoon-like from the side. Much longer and more tapered than the shorter, rounder bills of scaup or ring-necked ducks.

habitat: Canvasbacks prefer large, open bodies of water in New England, especially coastal bays, harbors, and the larger inland lakes. Look for them in deeper waters where they can dive for aquatic vegetation and mollusks - they're less common on small ponds or shallow wetlands. During migration, they often gather in protected marine waters like Long Island Sound or large lakes like Winnipesaukee.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in March and early April. Look for small flocks or pairs in larger bodies of water as they head north to breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Rare in New England during breeding season, as most nest in prairie pothole regions of the upper Midwest and Canada. Occasional non-breeding birds may linger.
seasonality.fall: First migrants appear in October, with numbers building through November. Males are in their brightest plumage during this time.
seasonality.winter: Most reliable season to find canvasbacks, especially in coastal waters and ice-free portions of larger lakes. They often form loose flocks with other diving ducks.

funFact: Canvasbacks are such powerful divers they can plunge down 30 feet underwater and have been found tangled in fishing nets set at depths of 100 feet - deeper than most scuba divers ever go!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with redheads, which have similar rusty-red heads on males. Remember: canvasbacks have the distinctive sloping 'ski jump' head profile and canvas-gray backs, while redheads have a more rounded head with a steeper forehead and darker gray backs. Think 'Canvas = sloping like a sail in the wind.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called North America's largest diving duck, canvasbacks were once much more common and were considered the ultimate prize by market hunters in the 1800s. Their populations crashed due to overhunting and wetland loss, making them a conservation success story as numbers have recovered with protection.
compareHints: Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares. Redheads are closest in size and male coloring, but have rounded heads and darker backs. Canvasbacks also sit higher on the water and appear more elongated than their chunkier cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring.
Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back.
Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes.

Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes.
